findings.text: The viewer plist runs without `-owner-code`, so it uses the default `auto`. In `auto`, if the dialog fails, the code goes to stderr (owner.go:73-78: "the terminal when there is none or it fails"). Under launchd, stderr goes to `$XDG_STATE_HOME/ai-workflow-engine/logs/viewer.log`, a file any local agent can read. An agent could then call `/owner/code` on loopback and take the owner credential for every O route. The plist must pin `-owner-code dialog`, and a Must not line should say the code never reaches a log file.

D-1 says "a test keeps a stand-in existing config byte-identical", and the design says check and service always pass `--config` for the factory's own file. No acceptance criterion covers either. The one decision that protects the owner's other live tunnel can pass the gate with no test behind it. Add an AC: setup, `--write-config`, service install and check run against a stand-in `~/.cloudflared/config.yml`, and the file stays byte-identical. The cloudflared plist must carry `--config <factory file>`.

The design says an agent's `--load` is refused only "when the worker guard knows the caller as an agent" (`whoAmI`/`RoleWorker`). Leads and the CEO session are agents too, and they run issue-cli in the same tmux and HOME. Nothing says they are refused. No Must not line says "agents never load, unload or bootstrap a LaunchAgent". The check also covers `launchctl bootout` on `--unload`, which can stop the owner's services. Name the lead and CEO roles in the refusal, add the Must not line, and add a test that a lead's `--load` and `--unload` are refused.

AC4 tests only `approve`. The phone pages the owner will use post to other owner routes: the YOLO review's Agree/Back to, the clarify form, post-mortem decide, shelf review and comments, owner-checks tick, and the CEO chat message box. The claim that every public request counts as the owner rests on `fromOwner` (owner.go:201-204). No test runs one owner route per page through a public token. AC4 should iterate `ownerOnlyRoute` the way TestOwnerRoutesRefuse… does.

Check 7 marks ✓ when the record's version string equals `issue-viewer -version`. The record proves only that some checkout with that `git describe` passed. A dirty tree or a rebuild that keeps the same tag also matches. The record should carry the commit plus a dirty flag, or the binary's hash, and the check should say ✗ on `dev`/dirty.

The busy-port refusal stops the owner's running viewer from being restarted. Nothing covers a viewer started by KeepAlive that later crash-loops on a port clash, for example when the owner starts one by hand again. Nothing covers `uninstall` without `--unload` either: it removes the plist and leaves a loaded service running with no file. `status` should report a loaded label with no plist, and `uninstall` should refuse while the label is loaded unless `--unload` is given.

Check 5 accepts "a 30x to `*.cloudflareaccess.com`" by suffix. It should match the configured `identity: team_domain` exactly, so a redirect to another team's Access (a wrong account) isn't counted ✓.
The plist captures the installer's whole PATH. If install runs from a shell with a sandbox or scratch PATH, the service keeps it for good. Status could print the PATH it carries.
The Access session length and policy scope are named as unverifiable. That is honest, and the viewer's own owner-email check is the backstop.

findings.text: The owner ran the steps and found that `cloudflared tunnel route dns factory factory.example-owner.com` made the CNAME `factory.example-owner.com.private-project.app`. This happens because the shared cert.pem is scoped to the other tunnel's zone (comment id 5). The Approach still tells the owner to skip login because the cert is shared (step 2) and then run `route dns` (step 4), which is the exact step that failed. So `remote setup` as designed prints steps known to be wrong. No step, check item or AC covers the comment's asks: the dashboard CNAME step to `<id>.cfargotunnel.com`, check resolving the name and flagging a record in another zone, the cloudflared version. There is also a conflict to settle first: telling the cert's zone apart from the name's zone means reading cert.pem, and step 2 says it is "checked with stat, never read". The design must say how the zone is found without reading the credential (for example, always print the dashboard CNAME step when cert.pem already exists).

The "after the critic" fix says AC4 covers every route in `ownerRoutes` through `Routes()` with a public token. The acceptance criterion itself still checks only "an owner decision (an approve)". The checkbox the gate reads can pass without the per-route test. Phone pages post to many other O routes (YOLO Agree/Back to, clarify, shelf review, CEO chat paste). A regression in any of them would ship unseen. Reword line 50 to iterate `ownerRoutes`: each one passes with a valid owner token and gets 403 with no token or a non-owner token.

Nothing says what must never happen on the public name for the paths that are new here. Add Must not lines: `POST /owner/code` and `/owner/pair` on a public request never mint a code or open a dialog (no test today asserts the 400 and that no dialog runner was called). No public request's Access identity is ever turned into an `iv_owner` loopback cookie. The CEO chat paste route, which types into an agent's session, stays behind the same verified-token gate with no extra bypass.

The agent refusal rests on env markers (`AGENT_NAME`, `CLAUDECODE`) and `whoAmI`, and any agent shell can drop these. There is also no `--quote`/owner-words requirement like the one `dispatch` and `job auto` use. Then, setup step 8 tells the owner to run `remote service install --load`. If they paste it into the CEO chat, the refusal blocks them, and nothing says to run it in their own terminal. Either require `--quote` with the owner's words, or state in step 8's output that it must run outside Claude Code.

The busy-port refusal turns the cutover into a gap the tool never closes. The owner must stop the 8090 viewer by hand, then `--load` starts a KeepAlive viewer on `<port>`. Nothing says which port the plist pins when viewer.json is absent (no viewer running), or what happens when viewer.json names a sandbox viewer (`-record-viewer`). A wrong port gives a tunnel pointing at nothing, and check item 3 would still be ✓ because it compares against the same wrong port. State the port's source and its fallback, and have check compare it against the plist's `-port`.

The tunnel already exists (id da6a8a93-…, comment id 5), but `--tunnel-id` is optional. Without it, the config has no `credentials-file`. cloudflared then has to resolve the name through cert.pem, which belongs to the other zone, so the run may depend on the other tunnel's login. Either make `--tunnel-id` required for `--write-config`, or have check item 3 flag a missing `credentials-file`.

The policy's email list and the session length can't be verified (the design says so). The only thing standing in for them is the owner's AC on line 53. Worth printing them as an explicit "unverified" line in `remote check` so a ✓ run isn't read as covering them.

The settled rules cited (Secrets are references, projects.yaml byte for byte) match the design: nothing writes projects.yaml, and credentials stay as paths. The cert.pem zone question in the first block is the one place that pressure falls on "never read".

report.coverage: read 2 of 2 files (the issue in full, docs/departments.md searched for the cited rules at lines 22 and 30), plus main.go:54 to confirm `-version` exists

findings.text: Line 165 cites the settled rule "Private projects stay private" and promises the existing tunnel's project is never named. The issue file breaks that promise itself. D-1 (line 189) quotes the owner naming the private project. Line 184 writes out the owner's real tunnel UUID, which is also the name of the credentials file. Comment 5 names the other zone. The issue file sits in the engine's issues/ tree, so tests, docs and commits will copy it from there. The design needs to scrub these, replacing them with "an existing tunnel" and `<tunnel-id>`. It also needs a Must not line: no real tunnel id, zone or private project name goes into code, tests, docs or the issue.

Two Must not lines have no acceptance criterion. Line 48: an Access identity never becomes an `iv_owner` cookie. Line 49: no route gets a public bypass, `lead/send` and the X routes included. AC 54 only goes over `ownerRoutes`. Add a test: a public request with a valid token gets no `Set-Cookie: iv_owner` on any route. Add a second test: every route in `Routes()` answers 403 to a public request with no token, not just the O routes.

The DNS logic rests on two guesses that nothing backs up. First, `<apex>` is taken as "the name's last two labels", which is wrong for zones like `example.co.uk`. Second, any name that resolves as `<name>.<other zone>` is called a stray record. If that other zone has a wildcard record, which is common on an app domain, check item 9 shows ✗ forever and the owner can't fix it. Item 9 should say how it treats a wildcard, for example by comparing against a random label in the same zone. The apex rule needs a source or a `--zone` flag.

The first critic run raised a case that is still open. A KeepAlive viewer is installed, then the owner starts a viewer by hand on the same port, or the reverse happens. launchd then restarts the losing viewer in a loop and fills `viewer.log`. The busy-port refusal only runs when the services are loaded. `status` and `check` should flag a service in a crash loop or a port held by a process other than the service, and docs/remote.md should say how to switch from one viewer to the other.

Check item 7 trusts `security-check.json` in `$XDG_STATE_HOME`. Any process running as the same user can write that file, agents included, so a ✓ only shows that the file says green. Lines 186 and 186's "Known gaps" already admit the same-user gap. Item 7's ✓ line should say what it can't prove, or the record should be tied to the binary's hash.

"The docs page exists" can't fail in any useful way. Name what the page must contain, for example the steps for a cert from another zone and the no-second-login warning. Or point it at a test, such as a docs link check that the pointers in getting-started and security.md resolve.

Every Clarify answer, Q1 included (which credential acts as the owner on the public name), is "assumed — YOLO", and D-1 is provisional. The security model is going into backlog with no owner stamp, so the YOLO review after the fact has to look at Q1 on purpose.

Check item 4 reads `launchctl print` output (`state = running`), which has no documented format. Item 5 matches the redirect against `team_domain` exactly, so it needs `team_domain` normalised first (scheme, trailing slash). Both should go behind the parser seams with fixtures.

findings.text: The design makes the owner's real domain the default `--name` (`factory.example-owner.com`, lines 21/22/103), and AC 53's test runs with `--name factory.example-owner.com`. That puts the real domain into code and tests, which the Must not on line 51 forbids ("no … domain other than placeholders … into code, tests, fixtures, docs, commits"). The slug carries the domain too (`…factory-example-owner-com…`), and so do the branch name and any `Issue:`/`Proves:` trailer that names the slug, so commits leak it as well. Either the default becomes a placeholder or required flag (e.g. no default, or `factory.<your domain>`) and AC 53 uses `factory.example.com`, or line 51 has to be relaxed by an owner decision. As written, the AC and the Must not can't both pass.

Check item 5 accepts a 403 as ✓. But the viewer's own identity gate answers 403 to any public request with no token (line 72, identity.go). So with no Access application at all, the tunnel passes straight to the viewer, the viewer says 403, and item 5 shows ✓. Line 80 says this check catches "a tunnel or Access policy that is set up wrong", but it can't tell "Access guards the name" from "Access is missing and the viewer refused". The owner sees all ✓ and then gets 403 on the phone. Item 5 should accept only Access's own answer: the redirect to `https://<team_domain>/`, or a 403 that carries Access's markers rather than the viewer's body or headers. A 403 from the viewer should be ✗ with the fix "create the Access application". The test for this case needs a stand-in that answers like the viewer.

"`--load` refuses while the port answers" doesn't say whose listener counts. After the first install, the port is held by our own KeepAlive service. Re-running `install --load`, for example after `make install` or after a crash, is then refused with "stop the viewer you run by hand", which is the wrong advice. Line 196 already has the listener-pid vs service-pid reading, so the refusal should use it. Nothing covers a partial `--load` either: the viewer bootstraps and then cloudflared fails, or the other way round. There's no rollback or retry rule, and `status` and `check` don't name that half-loaded state.

The viewer plist's ProgramArguments (line 128) don't include `-owner-code dialog`. Only the later "after the critic" note (line 172) and the Must not (line 43) add it. In `auto` mode the code goes to stderr when the dialog fails (owner.go:100-105), so the plist arguments the implementer copies from the Approach would send the code into viewer.log. Line 128 should list the full argv, with `-owner-code dialog` in it.

Q1 sets the security model: a verified Access identity is the owner for every O route, including `lead/send`, which pastes into agent sessions. Its answer is "assumed — YOLO", not the owner's words. The YOLO review after the fact and the owner box AC 59 do cover it, but the owner should confirm Q1 before the name goes public, not after.
`-config` and `-version` exist on issue-viewer (main.go:49,54), so the plist argv and check item 7 rest on real flags.

report.coverage: read 2 of 2 files (the issue in full with its comments; docs/departments.md searched for the settled rules it cites, lines 22 and 30), plus main.go flag definitions and owner.go:70-106

findings.text: The design keeps viewer state (`push/subscriptions.json`, `settings.json`, `sent.jsonl`) in the state dir. That goes against the settled rule at docs/departments.md:25, which says "the viewer holds no state of its own". The issue argues the rule covers only goals, outputs and checks, but that is the author's own reading. docs/departments.md:20 says a rule changes "only by a new decision on the issue that changes it, and then this list changes with it". The issue has no `## Decisions` and no D-n for this. Q5 is only "assumed — YOLO", and no edit to docs/departments.md is planned. Record a decision that narrows the rule (device state may live in the state dir; business data may not) and plan the docs/departments.md edit, or the work breaks a settled rule.

The ledger can't hold the retry and multi-device cases it promises. It is keyed by event alone (`<project>|<kind>|<slug>|…`), and "A key already in `sent.jsonl` is skipped". Two problems follow. First, a 429/5xx that should be retried "at most 3 times" either lands in sent.jsonl and is skipped for good, or never lands there and has no counter; the design doesn't say which, and neither works as written. Second, with two devices (phone + desktop, line 21), a partial failure (one 201, one 429 or 410) can't be recorded per device. Either the event goes out again to the device that already got it (breaking "Each event is sent once"), or the failed device never gets it. The key needs to be per (event, subscription), with an attempt count. A test should cover two subscriptions where one answers 201 and the other 503.

Gate keys carry the target but no `Since`. An issue that reaches the same gate a second time (Send back for fixes, then back to the same gate) builds the same key. That key is already in sent.jsonl, so the owner is never pinged again for the next 30 days, which is exactly the "gate sits for hours" case this issue exists to fix. Line 56 gives `Since` as the cure for things that come back, but that applies only to CI and questions. Add `Since` (or the stamp's round) to the gate key, and add a test where a gate is reached twice and sends twice.

`Topic` is set to "the event key's hash". RFC 8030 §5.4 caps Topic at 32 base64url characters, and a base64url SHA-256 is 43, so push services can refuse the request. State the encoding and length (for example, a truncated 24-byte hash), and have the httptest stand-in reject a Topic over 32 characters so a test can fail.

No Must-not line says that subscription endpoints and keys are never shown or logged. Line 81 itself calls an endpoint a capability URL. Yet `/push` is an R route that lists "devices", and line 125 adds a startup log line naming the state dir. Add: "Endpoints, `p256dh` and `auth` never appear on a page, in a log, in status.md or in JSON; devices show only their label and date." Back it with a test on `/push`'s HTML.

Seeding runs "after a subscribe, or with an empty ledger". The ledger empties itself: entries older than 30 days are dropped (line 80), and on a quiet board that can leave nothing. Any wait that lands just before such a scan would then be seeded silently instead of pushed. Seeding is also not tied to a single subscription, so when a second device subscribes, events that are pending a retry for the first device may be marked seeded. Make seeding depend on a "seeded once" marker per subscription, not on the ledger being empty.

The quiet-hours digest is not covered. Nothing says what happens when the viewer is stopped across the end of the quiet window: is the digest sent at the next start, or lost? Nothing says whether muted projects count in "N", or whether items resolved during the night still count. There is also no test where the quiet window crosses midnight (line 55). Line 35's acceptance criterion would pass without any of these.

The CSP claim holds. headers.go:21's basePolicy has no default-src, and csp.go:58 adds `script-src 'self' 'nonce-…'`, so `/sw.js` (through worker-src → script-src) and the manifest load. On the public name, `fromOwner` accepts the verified Access identity (owner.go:201-203), so the phone can subscribe away from the desk without the desk-only sign-in code. The issue should say so on /push.

The payload is encrypted end to end, but the title (an issue title) and the project name appear on the phone's lock screen. Under the settled rule "Private projects stay private" (docs/departments.md:23), consider a per-project setting that shows "<kind> in a private project" with no title.

report.coverage: read 2 of 2 files (the issue in full, docs/departments.md's Settled rules section), plus the CSP and fromOwner lines in csp.go, headers.go and owner.go to check claims.

findings.text: Nothing stops two writers from overwriting each other's ledger changes. The subscribe handler seeds the new device into `events.json` (line 89), and the 60 s scan reads and writes the same file. "Written aside and renamed" (line 77) makes each write whole, but it doesn't stop one write from wiping out the other. Take a scan that loaded the ledger before a subscribe and saves after it. Its save drops the new device's `seeded` entries, so the next scan pushes everything waiting to the new phone: the flood that Q3 and line 51 rule out. Two viewers sharing a state dir have the same problem, because `sender.lock` (line 93) only guards sending, and either viewer's `/push/subscribe` and `/push/settings` still write `subscriptions.json`, `settings.json` and `events.json`. One lock (or one owner goroutine) is needed for every read-modify-write of `push/`, plus a test where a subscribe lands during a scan.

On the public name, the browser probably won't be able to load the app shell. The issue says that name works over Cloudflare Access, and the viewer answers 403 to any public request without a verified `Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion` (identity.go:42-56, fromOwner owner.go:201). Browsers fetch `<link rel="manifest">` without credentials unless it has `crossorigin="use-credentials"`, and the design doesn't mention that attribute. The Access cookie isn't sent, so Access redirects to its login page or the gate answers 403. The manifest then fails, and iOS doesn't add the site as a `standalone` app. Line 48 says iOS sends Web Push only to such an app. The design doesn't cover how `/sw.js`, the icons and `apple-touch-icon` get past Access either. The playtest (line 139) runs on loopback, so it can't catch this. Say how each shell resource gets through Access and the identity gate, or why it doesn't need to, and test a public Host with no identity header.

The startup log line is given two ways. Secrecy (line 82) says `push: N devices`, with no path, and a test backs that. Discoverability (line 129) says `push: N devices subscribed (state dir …/push)`. Pick one. As line 129 stands, it either breaks the line 82 test or leaves a test that fails for the wrong reason.

The default VAPID `sub` is `mailto:owner@localhost` when there's no `allowed_hosts` entry, and nothing cites a source saying push services accept it. Apple's service checks the JWT `sub` and is known to answer 403 BadJwtToken for subjects it rejects. On a loopback-only viewer, every push to an iPhone could then come back `refused`. Lines 34 and 137 both use a stand-in that accepts any `sub`, so no test could catch this. Cite what Apple, FCM and Mozilla accept, or require a real contact, and show on /push when it's missing.

An event only closes after it has been gone for 2 scans or 5 minutes, whichever is longer. So a gate reached again within 5 minutes of Send back for fixes, or a new `question:` within 5 minutes of answering the last one, sends nothing. A quick fix-and-return is exactly that case. The line 137 test ("a gate closed (Send back) and reached again sends again") passes only if it waits past the window. Pin the window in that test, or say the miss is accepted.

Issue titles from private projects will show on a locked phone's screen. The rule at docs/departments.md:23 is about repo content, so this doesn't break it. The payload is end-to-end encrypted (RFC 8291), so the push services can't read it.

report.coverage: read 2 of 2 files (the issue in full, docs/departments.md's Settled rules lines 18-38), plus fromOwner (owner.go:201), basePolicy (headers.go:21), the script CSP (csp.go:58) and publicRequest (identity.go:35-56) to check claims.

findings.text: The first Must not forbids rewriting any existing D-n line. Yet child 1's `decide --amend D-n` "rewrites text or attributes in place", and child 9 amends the Settled rules' source lines in done issues. As written, the Must not rules out two children, and child 9 can't be built without breaking it. The design needs to say exactly what may change in place: for example, only the trailing `{…}` attribute group may be added or changed, the text and quote stay byte for byte, and changing the text goes through `--replaces`. As it stands, `--amend` can silently change an owner-quoted decision that other issues cite by ref.

The diff audit passes a branch that touches a hard decision's `paths:` if the issue merely cites the ref, or writes `n/a <ref>: <why>`, or has an open challenge. Agents can open challenges themselves (`decision challenge`), and `decision_unchallenged` only holds issues that *cite* the challenged decision. So a worker can challenge without citing, touch the guarded paths, and pass both validators before the owner answers. Typing the ref proves the agent saw the decision, not that it followed it. That empties the exit "a change against a hard decision can't pass a gate unnoticed": the gate should hold while a challenge on a touched hard decision is open, whether or not the issue cites it. A Must not should rule out an agent's own `n/a` clearing a hard decision whose paths the branch touches.

Six Clarify answers are marked "assumed — YOLO", but the issue has no `## Decisions` section and no D-n lines. The clarify round is supposed to turn each answer into a D-n via `tracker.AnswerQuestion`. Because of that, the epic's key choices (the attribute group on the line, legacy lines read as `issue`/soft, the path-based gate, owner-only hard) can't be cited, can't be challenged and can't be scoped by the ledger this epic builds. Child 3's own validator would have no ref to cite for them. They are also invisible to the YOLO after-the-fact review. Record them as provisional D-n decisions before the children are filed.

The block caps at 12 lines with hard decisions first, yet child 3 requires citing *every* hard in-force decision. Child 9 makes the Settled rules hard and mostly project-scoped, and docs/departments.md:18-40 has about 20 rules citing more than 30 refs. So on day one the hard set can exceed 12: the agent must cite decisions the block folded into a count, and the block is all Settled rules. Say how the cap treats hard decisions (never fold hard ones, or `decisions_cited` covers only what was shown plus the command), and add a test at more than 12 hard.

Child 9 assumes every Settled rule has a D-n source with recorded owner words. Some don't: docs/departments.md:25 and 28 cite "factory/department-role-and-goals (values log)" and "factory/global-screens" with no ref, and docs/departments.md:29 cites a playtest finding. Rules decided under YOLO are provisional, so Must not 108 forbids making them hard. Child 9 needs a criterion for a rule with no ref or no owner words (left soft and listed, never made hard by an agent). It also needs to say who may edit another done issue's file, given the worker guard "you work on <slug> only".

No command could fail these criteria as stated. "Covering every part the roadmap names" and "the roadmap's 0.60 row says what shipped" have no check, and none of the three tests the exit at line 36. Add criteria a test can fail: a dispatched worker's prompt contains a project-scoped hard decision from another issue, and a branch touching a hard decision's `paths:` without citing it is refused at `in progress → testing`.

`.decisions/log.jsonl` gets an `injected` event per briefing from parallel workers and leads, but nothing says it is appended under a lock or in one atomic write, or how its growth is bounded. "Drops out of force the day after" also doesn't name a clock or timezone for gates versus briefings. These are the "two callers at once" and boundary cases children 1, 2 and 7 should test.

report.coverage: read 2 of 2 files (the issue in full; docs/departments.md's Settled rules and the sections that match the design's terms)

findings.text: Viewers with different project sets that share one state dir will break dedup and push fake rows to the owner's phone. The design assumes every viewer on `push/` sees the same board. Under CLAUDE.md, `make ux-test`, playtests and hand-started sandbox viewers run against throwaway scenario boards (the `-record-viewer` and sandbox-viewer notes). They keep the default `$XDG_STATE_HOME` unless someone isolates it. Such a viewer takes the same flock, reads the owner's real `subscriptions.json` and pushes its scenario rows to the real phone. That breaks line 29 ("Test with a sandbox"), because the sandbox sends for real. Its scans also see none of the owner's real keys. After 2 scans it closes them, the real viewer opens them again, and each comes back as a new event and is pushed again. So the work fails line 25's "each event is sent once" every few minutes. Fixes needed: an event's key and its closing should be limited to the projects the scanning viewer loaded (a project another viewer owns is never closed by this one). A sandbox viewer (temp-folder config, or not the recorded viewer, the same test `-record-viewer` uses) should never send. A test should run two viewers with different project sets on one state dir.

The claim that the hold "is bounded" has no limit behind it. The scan holds the store lock across every send, and each send can take up to 10 s, so the hold grows with events × devices. Two cases make that large: a push service outage (every `retry` delivery is tried again on every scan) and the first scan after quiet hours or a restart. A `/push/subscribe` or `/push/settings` POST waits behind it and can hit the server's write timeout (main.go). The owner then sees a failed Subscribe for something that is in fact only queued. Either send outside the lock (decide and mark under the lock, send, then save the results under the lock) or set a cap per scan. Then test a subscribe that lands during a slow scan.

`AllowedEndpoint` checks only the stored URL. Go's `http.Client` follows 307/308 redirects on a POST and keeps the body. A redirect from an allowed host (or from a forged subscription to a lookalike name that passes a loose `*.push.apple.com` suffix match) can therefore reach any URL, which is the SSRF the allow-list exists to stop. Say that `CheckRedirect` refuses every redirect and that the match is on the exact host or a dot-suffix (`.push.apple.com`, not a bare string suffix). Add a stand-in that answers 307 and a test showing it is refused.

A device can stop getting notifications and nobody is told. On 404/410 the device is removed without a word. The service worker doesn't handle `pushsubscriptionchange`, which browsers fire when they rotate a subscription. The owner's phone then goes quiet with nothing on /push, and Needs you shows no warning, which brings back the "gate sits for hours" case. The service worker should re-subscribe on `pushsubscriptionchange`. /push and the `Push:` line in status.md should show "device removed by the push service on <date>".

A "worker stuck" event flaps. Workers sit at a prompt for a moment and then go on working all the time. Each idle-at-menu that lasts past `agentIdleAfter`, then clears for 2 scans and comes back, is a new key (the session), so it is a new push. One worker can ping the phone many times an hour. Add a minimum stuck time, or a cooldown per session, and a test where a worker idles, works and idles again.

No acceptance criterion backs either Must not. Nothing in AC1–AC5 would fail if an endpoint or key appeared on `/push`, in JSON or in a log (line 31), or if a payload carried a home path or note (line 28). Those tests are only in the "sketch" test plan (line 145), which line 143 says is decided later. Add an acceptance criterion for each.

The route table (line 115) lists three shell paths. D-2 (line 183) and line 106 exempt four, and the table leaves out `/apple-touch-icon.png`, which security.md's inventory is meant to copy. The claims that iOS sends no cookies for the touch icon and does send them for a `use-credentials` manifest at Add to Home Screen also have no source. Cite one, or say the public-Host playtest on a real iPhone (AC5) is what checks them.

The payload is encrypted end to end, but it is shown on a locked phone. Issue titles from a project with `privacy: work_files: tracker` would show on the lock screen. The owner may want a per-project "title hidden" option, and that is worth asking about.

findings.text: Any agent can stop every gate in the project with one command. Child 3 makes every issue cite every hard decision in force. Child 9 makes the Settled rules hard and mostly project-scoped. Child 4's `decision_unchallenged` then holds the gate of any issue that cites a decision with an open challenge, from any challenger, until the owner resolves it. So one worker's `decision challenge` on a project-wide hard decision holds every issue in the project. Under YOLO, with the owner away, the factory stops. The design needs to say what a challenge holds: only the challenger's issue, plus issues whose branch touches that decision's `paths:`. It also needs a test where a challenge on decision A does not hold an unrelated issue that only cites A.

Nothing enforces "only the owner's words". `hard` relies on `NeedsOwnerWords`, which checks that a non-provisional quote is on the line, and an agent can type any `--quote`. `decision resolve <ref>` (line 73) is a plain CLI command with no owner check at all. A worker held by `decision_unchallenged` or `decisions_respected` can run `decision resolve` itself, or record a decision hard with a quote it made up. That breaks Must not 112 and the exit at line 37. Name the check, as other features do (`fromOwnerBrowser`, an owner-only route, or the agents-refused rule in `proof.OwnerTicks`), and add an acceptance test where an agent's `decision resolve` and `--hard` are both refused.

The diff audit only sees decisions "in force" for the issue being checked, through `InForce(index, issue, status)`, which filters by scope and `at:`. Take a hard decision scoped `system:Workflow` with `paths: cmd/issue-cli/**`, or one with `at: in design`. A branch on a UI issue that rewrites those files passes `in progress → testing` without anyone noticing, because the decision is not in force for that issue at that status. Scope decides who gets briefed. It should not decide which branches the path guard skips. As written, the exit's "can't pass a gate unnoticed" fails. `paths:` should be checked against every hard decision, whatever its scope or `at:`. Criterion 29 should include an issue whose system is outside the decision's scope.

Nothing covers two writers at once. Many workers append `injected` and `challenged` events to `<issues>/.decisions/log.jsonl`, and the lead's `decide --amend` rewrites the D-n lines of other issues' files while those issues' workers may be writing the same files. Say there is a lock, or an append-only write and an atomic rename for the line splice (the way `internal/queue` uses Update under a lock), and give child 1 a criterion that two concurrent amends or appends lose nothing.

Child 2 records `injected` events from `show` and from the command that prints the critic's brief. That makes read commands write, including the critic's own read-only run. The log also grows with every `show` call, and child 6's "injected per briefing" counts get inflated. Log only real briefings (dispatch, `start`, lead spawn), or say that `show` and the critic's brief never write.

The epic-level tests leave out things the design depends on: that hard decisions are never folded when there are more than 12, and that an agent's own challenge does not clear the diff audit. "The branch diff against its base" is also undefined after a `chore(merge)` of main. Say it is the merge-base three-dot diff, so files main changed don't count as the branch touching a decision's paths.

All six decisions behind the epic are YOLO provisional (D-1..D-6), and so is every key choice in it: the record lives on the line, legacy lines are issue/soft, the gate is path-based, and only the owner makes a decision hard. By the epic's own rule, none of these can be hard until the owner confirms them, so the ledger's design rules are themselves only soft once it ships.

Line 20 says the Settled rules were settled by "the owner and the lead". Lines 25, 28 and 29 cite sources with no D-n ref. Expect child 9 to leave a large share of the rules soft and listed for the owner, so on day one the block will hold fewer hard decisions than the design suggests.

findings.text: The design gives two rules for the event key. Line 57 says a row that returns is a new event "because its key carries `Since`". Line 88 says the key is `<project>|<kind>|<slug>|<target>` and "nothing depends on a file's mtime". An implementer who follows line 57 breaks "each event is sent once" (line 25). When `Since` is approximate, it is the issue file's mtime (attention.go:64), so every edit to a waiting issue makes a new key and sends again. Delete line 57's `Since` claim, or restate it as presence (closed for 2 scans, then reopened). Add a test that edits a waiting issue and checks that nothing is sent.

`settings.json`'s `config` binding doesn't say who sets it the first time, or how it is ever rebound. A hand-started sandbox viewer can claim viewer.json while the 8090 viewer is down. If that happens on first use, `push/` is bound to the sandbox's temp config. The owner's real viewer then gets 409 for good, and nothing on the page says how to fix it. The same thing happens when the owner moves projects.yaml. Say that only a non-sandbox config binds (not a temp folder), and give an owner-only rebind on /push.

The quiet-hours digest has no failure path. It isn't an event in the ledger, so nothing says what happens when it gets a 503 or 410: is it retried, how many times, and do the `quiet` deliveries stay `quiet`? Line 96 says "a `sending` left by a crash counts as `retry`". So after a crash during the digest scan, the held events would go out one push each instead of as one digest. Give the digest its own delivery record and retry rule, and test a 503 and a crash during the digest.

No acceptance criterion backs "only the recorded viewer sends" or the shared lock. Both appear only in the design and the "sketch" test plan (line 146). The Must not at line 29 (never touch the 8090 viewer, test with a sandbox) depends on them. As the criteria stand, they would all pass while a sandbox viewer sharing the state dir pushes scenario rows to the owner's real phone. Add an AC for each: two viewers on one state dir, and a subscribe that lands during a scan.

D-2 lets `/static/icons/*` through the identity gate with a wildcard. The design doesn't say the match is on the cleaned path, only for GET and HEAD, and only for files that exist. A prefix check on the raw path (`/static/icons/../…`, or a POST) is the kind of hole that turns a narrow exemption into a bypass. Say how the match is made. Add tests for `..`, encoded slashes and a non-GET method on a public Host.

`pushsubscriptionchange` re-subscribes with the `iv_owner` session. owner.go keeps that session in memory only, so any viewer restart before the browser rotates the subscription loses the device. Line 102 accepts this, but in practice a removed device after each restart will be the usual case on loopback, not a rare one. On the public name, `fromOwner` accepts the Access identity (owner.go:202), so this doesn't happen there.

The payload title is an issue title, so it can name a private project's client on the lock screen (docs/departments.md:23, "Private projects stay private"). The push itself is end-to-end encrypted. A per-project "hide titles" option, or showing only the kind for private projects, could be worth a decision.

findings.text: An agent can weaken a hard decision as easily as it could make one, and nothing stops it. Line 67 and Must not 121 make only four acts owner-only: marking a decision hard, resolving a challenge, renewing an expired one, letting one go. Line 73 asks for the owner's words only when a group is made `hard`. So a worker held by `decisions_respected` can do any of these: run `decide --amend D-n` to drop `hard`, empty `paths:` or add a past `expires:`; or run `decide --replaces <ref>` with a soft D-m. Each takes the decision out of force or out of the guard, and the next transition passes. The design also never says whether a D-m made by `--replaces` keeps the replaced line's hard flag and `paths:`. That empties the exit "a change against a hard decision can't pass a gate unnoticed". Any amend that removes or narrows `hard`, `paths:` or `expires:` on a hard decision, and any `--replaces` of one, should be owner-only. Add a test that refuses each of these from an agent session.

Child 9 can't be built under the epic's own rules. It has "the lead run the amends on other issues' files", setting `hard` on the Settled rules' sources. But line 67 and Must not 121 refuse `hard` from every agent session, "the lead included". The design also contradicts itself on the lead. Q5's chosen answer (D-5's source) says "the lead relays the owner's quote", and docs/departments.md:166 says owner words normally arrive that way (`--quote` through the lead). Line 67, though, accepts the owner's words only from the owner's own shell or their browser. Pick one: either the owner runs child 9's amend list themselves (a Needs you row or the Decisions log's Hard option), or the lead may relay an existing owner quote. Then make child 9's criteria and D-5 say the same.

The diff audit checks "any hard decision in the project", with no exception for replaced or expired ones. Child 3's `citations_current` refuses any cited ref that is replaced or expired. If a branch touches the `paths:` of a replaced hard decision, the issue has to cite it to pass one validator and must not cite it to pass the other, so the gate can never pass. Say that the audit covers only hard decisions that are active, not replaced and not expired. Pair that with the inheritance rule from the first finding, so a replacement doesn't silently drop the guard.

The new attribute group is a trailing `{…}`, and that collides with old lines. Existing D-n text and quotes already contain braces at the end, for example `{from: <dept>, to: product, via: hq}` (docs/departments.md:36). This issue's own D-2 (line 163) has a `{scope: …; hard; …}` group inside its text. The design doesn't say what happens with a trailing brace group that isn't a valid attribute group: is it text, an error, or an "unknown key" for lint (line 87)? Must not 119 ("old lines parse as they did") needs a child-1 criterion: a legacy line ending in a brace group that isn't an attribute group parses exactly as before, and a group is recognised only after the closing quote or the `(replaces …)` part.

No command can fail these two criteria as written, and an earlier critique already flagged them. "Covering every part the roadmap names" and "the roadmap's 0.60 row says what shipped" need a check. One option: a table mapping each part named at line 42 to the child that builds it, and a lint or grep that the 0.60 row names each child.

For `decide --amend`, the old group's only record is the audit log line, yet the design doesn't order the two writes. If the D-n line is spliced and the log append then fails, the history is lost. It would help to say the log is written first, or that a failed append undoes the splice. The log also grows by one `injected` line per briefing and nothing caps it.

When child 3 adds `decisions_cited` to the bundled templates, issues already in design start being refused at their next gate. Projects that take the `decision-ledger` upgrade get the same refusal. A sentence on in-flight issues would help, for example "applies to issues entering design after adoption", or "n/a lines accepted".

findings.text: The design never says how YOLO treats the new holds, and the board runs under YOLO right now (all six Clarify answers say "assumed — YOLO"). YOLO lets gates pass without the owner and reviews them afterwards. Nothing says whether `decision_unchallenged`, `decisions_respected`'s open-challenge hold, or an expired hard decision's Renew / Let go row is an owner wait that YOLO passes or a hard stop. If YOLO passes them, the diff audit does nothing during YOLO windows, which breaks the exit "can't pass a gate unnoticed". If it doesn't, one open challenge on a hard decision with broad `paths:` stops every branch that touches those paths until the owner comes back. Pick one, record it as a D-n, and add a child criterion that walks the fixture gate with YOLO on.

"The audit log records who ran it … so the YOLO review sees every lead relay" has no mechanism and no child builds it. The YOLO review queue is built from comments (internal/yolo), not from `.decisions/log.jsonl`. So under YOLO a lead can type any `--quote` and make a decision hard, or drop `hard`, narrow `paths:` or add `expires:`, and the owner never sees it. Also, no epic acceptance criterion tests Must not 141 (a worker refused on `--hard`, `--amend` of a hard line, `--replaces`, `decision resolve`, renew). Add that test, and say which child puts lead-relayed hard-decision acts into the YOLO review queue (or a Needs you row).

A write is two steps: the locked body splice through `UpdateIssueBody`, then the locked log append. Nothing covers one succeeding and the other failing. Child 1 says the old attribute group is kept only in the audit log. If the append fails after the amend, the previous group is lost from the ledger and child 6's counts and child 8's drift read wrong history. Say the order (log the intent first, or restore the line when the append fails) and give child 1 a criterion for the failed append.

Any worker's `decision challenge` on a hard decision with wide `paths:` (for example `cmd/issue-cli/**`) holds other workers' branches that touch those paths, not only its own issue, until the owner answers. A worker can stall its peers with one command. Say whether opening a challenge that holds other issues is a lead or owner act, or whether only the challenger's issue is held and the others are flagged in the Needs you row.

The default `issue` scope includes "issues that cite it". So citing a hard issue-scoped decision puts it in force for the citing issue, and `decisions_cited` then requires the citation that put it there. That is harmless only while legacy lines stay soft. Child 1's InForce test should pin down this loop.

"Drops out of force the day after" names no timezone or clock source. The block's readability claim at line 52 also has no bound, because hard decisions are never folded and child 9 makes around 20 Settled rules hard.
